list.listitem: Four cardiac rhythms result in pulseless cardiac arrest: ventricular fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, asystole, and pulseless electrical activity.

Bystander recognition of sudden cardiac arrest, immediate activation of emergency medical services, and prompt initiation of lay-rescuer CPR with a focus on effective compressions improves survival. A

Early defibrillation of victims of ventricular fibrillation/pulseless ventricular tachycardia is critical. When an automated external defibrillator (AED) is on-site and accessible, it should be used as soon as possible. A
Advanced ACLS therapies, such as the insertion of an advanced airway or administration of medications to support circulation, have not been shown to increase survival to hospital discharge. A
Post-resuscitation care may include induced hypothermia in ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia victims, which may increase their chance of survival and neurologic recovery. B
Survivors of sudden cardiac arrest not due to a transient or reversible cause are candidates for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator. A
Cardiac arrest is the cessation of cardiac mechanical activity, which results in the absence of circulation and, without intervention, death.
Sudden cardiac death is defined as death from a cardiac cause that occurred within 1 hour of symptom onset in the out-of-hospital setting and without other probable causes of death.
More than 400,000 persons per year are estimated to die from sudden cardiac death.
Sudden cardiac death accounts for more than 50% of all cardiac deaths per year.
In 1998, the mean age of men who died of sudden cardiac death was 70 years; the mean age of women was 82.4 years.
The majority of unexpected cardiac deaths occur in persons without identifiable cardiovascular risk factors.
Patients taking antipsychotics are at increased risk.
Ventricular tachyarrhythmias account for approximately 85% of cardiac arrests.
Ventricular tachycardia progressing to ventricular fibrillation and finally to asystole is the most common arrhythmic sequence in cardiac arrest victims.

Acute ischemia is the most common initiating event. However, ventricular tachycardia often develops in or around an area of myocardial scar, most commonly from a prior myocardial infarction. In addition, ventricular tachycardia is the fatal arrhythmia in many less common inherited and acquired cardiac disorders (see ).
Bradyarrhythmias, asystole, or pulseless electrical activity may be the initiating rhythm of cardiac arrest in approximately 15% of patients. Most of these patients have advanced heart disease.
Survivors may describe chest discomfort, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, dizziness, or generalized weakness. However, there are often no premonitory symptoms.
Agonal respirations are common in cardiac arrest victims and should not preclude initiation of CPR.
Unconsciousness occurs quickly because of insufficient perfusion to the brain.

In a recent observational study published in 2023, they compared manual carotid pulse checks against carotid ultrasound; a total of 568 participants were analyzed and found that carotid ultrasound may be a superior tool to making accurate and timely decisions during CPR. It was determined to be 100% sensitive and 98% specific when compared to manual pulse check, 80% sensitive and 91% specific. In addition, carotid ultrasound was able to detect return of spontaneous circulation decision in 2.8 seconds versus 3 seconds with manual pulse check. All results were statistically significant.
Arrhythmias leading to pulseless arrest should be managed according to the ACC/AHA guidelines published elsewhere; the ACC/AHA algorithm is shown in .
Inpatient teams led by a specially trained physician assistant in a community hospital improved key clinical outcomes including mortality.
The universal compression:ventilation ratio of 30:2 is recommended for victims from infancy through adulthood if performed by a lone rescuer.
A 30:2 compressions:ventilation ratio is recommended for adult victims with 1-rescuer or 2-rescuer CPR and all lay rescuers.

A 15:2 compressions:ventilation ratio is recommended for 2-rescuer CPR for infants and children who have not reached puberty. This ratio allows more rescue breaths to be delivered to younger victims who have a higher rate of asphyxia arrest.
Rescuers are encouraged to allow complete chest recoil after each compression and to minimize interruptions in the delivery of compressions.

A Cochrane systematic review did not find any benefit to active chest compression-decompression (using a handheld suction device) in patients with cardiac arrest. There is insufficient data to suggest that mechanical devices for chest compression are more effective (or more harmful) than traditional chest compressions.
A systematic review concluded that the optimal depth of chest compressions is 40 to 55 mm, with the optimal depth being 45 mm.
Establishing an advanced airway (endotracheal tube, Combitube, LMA) has been de-emphasized in the updated resuscitation guidelines.

In addition, a study of in-hospital CPR revealed that in the majority of cases, victims receive excessive ventilation. This results in a decrease in venous return and a decrease in coronary and cerebral perfusion. One meta-analysis found that performance of bystander CPR resulted in slightly inferior outcomes relative to bystander of chest compressions alone.
A recent meta-analysis found that compression-only CPR was associated to similar outcomes as traditional CPR.

Each rescue breath should be delivered over 1 second and provide enough tidal volume to produce visible chest rise. Current recommendations for bystander CPR is to focus on chest compressions rather than rescue breathing (i.e., hands-only CPR).
Once an advanced airway is in place, 8 to 10 rescue breaths should be delivered per minute without interruption in chest compressions.

Two meta-analyses were conducted in 2022 and 2023 with regards to optimizing airway management strategies during a cardiac arrest. In 2022, 25 articles were compared, with a total of 196,486 patients, which concluded endotracheal intubation had better survival outcomes when implemented early during resuscitation efforts, when compared to supraglottic airway and bag-valve-mask ventilation. The second systematic review published in 2023, with 13,949 patients enrolled concluded that there was no difference in survival between endotracheal intubation and other modalities of ventilation.

Ventricular fibrillation is the most common rhythm documented in adults with witnessed cardiac arrest. Survival rates are highest when the victim receives prompt bystander CPR and is defibrillated in the first 3 to 5 minutes.
When an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest is witnessed and an AED is available, the AED should be utilized as quickly as possible.

When emergency medical personnel (EMS) arrive and ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia is present, the EMS rescuer should deliver 1 shock (instead of 3 stacked shocks) and then immediately resume compressions.

The rescuer should not recheck the rhythm or the pulse until after completing approximately 5 cycles or 2 minutes of CPR. Modern biphasic defibrillators have a high first shock efficacy averaging more than 90% (defined as termination of ventricular fibrillation for at least 5 seconds after the shock). Often after ventricular fibrillation is terminated, victims demonstrate a nonperfusing rhythm for several minutes, which necessitates immediate CPR.
Rescuers using monophasic defibrillators should administer an initial shock of 360 joules.
Defibrillation with biphasic devices requires less energy (120-200 joules) than monophasic defibrillators.

There is no human clinical trial evidence showing increased rates of survival to hospital discharge using vasopressors or antiarrhythmic drug therapy during cardiac arrest resuscitation attempts. Nonetheless, there is consensus that it is reasonable to continue to use vasopressors and antiarrhythmic therapy as indicated in the Advanced Cardiac Life Support algorithm in . Epinephrine and vasopressin remain the vasopressors of choice, supported by evidence from one large clinical trial.

A follow up meta-analysis done in 2022 with 6,609 participants found that there was no difference in outcomes with only vasopressin use, with outcomes defined as neurologic outcomes, in-hospital mortality or ventricular arrhythmias.

A meta-analysis published in 2023 showed that standard dose epinephrine, high dose epinephrine and epinephrine with vasopressin all helped achieve return of spontaneous circulation and improved survival until hospital admission but that effect did not extend to discharge with the exception of standard dose epinephrine, which did reveal survival to discharge in patients with initial nonshockable rhythm.

Amiodarone or lidocaine may be administered during a ventricular fibrillation/ventricular tachycardia pulseless arrest. A recent clinical trial showed not improvements in neurologic recovery or survivial when compared to placebo therapy, but there was a noted benefit in the subgroup with witnessed cardiac arrest.
Atropine may be administered during asystole or pulseless electrical activity.
For recommended dosages, routes of administration, and recommended medication sequences for specific cardiac arrest rhythms, please see the algorithm in .
Every effort should be made by the paramedic team in the field to adequately resuscitate the victim of sudden cardiac arrest, unless the patient's previously expressed wishes to forego CPR are known.
Decisions to terminate resuscitative efforts should be based on clinical judgment and human dignity; there are no set time limits or CPR cycles after which stopping resuscitation is indicated.

Sudden cardiac arrest victims who do not benefit from CPR/ACLS protocols on the scene with return of spontaneous circulation are very unlikely to benefit from transport to the emergency department (ED). Transport to the ED is acceptable if there are interventions in the hospital unavailable to the emergency medical team (eg, cardiopulmonary bypass or extracorporeal circulation) from which the patient might benefit.

Initial studies showed that by inducing hypothermia to 32 to 34ºC for 12 to 24 hours, using external cooling methods, has been shown to improve outcomes in comatose patients with return of spontaneous circulation after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
Hyperthermia should be avoided. An example of a therapeutic hypothermia protocol is shown in .

However, a large Swedish trial randomized 1900 adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and coma to targeted hypothermia at 33 C or to normothermia with early treatment of fever. It found no difference in 6 month outcomes. Patients with asystole as the initial rhythm and unwitnessed arrests.

Several systematic reviews were published with varying results regarding targeted temperature management. A study in 2022 with approximately 2900 patients, did not reveal an better survival or neurologic outcome when targeted temperature management was compared to normothermia. However, in 2023, another study with 5,218 patients enrolled compared hypothermia (defined 31 - 36ºC) and active normothermia (37ºC) showed improved neurological outcomes compared to patients who did not undergo targeted temperature management. Additionally, the patients who were cooled, received one of two treatments: intravenous cooling and surface cooling. A subgroup analysis showed that intravenous cooling was the better cooling method.

This was also supported by a more recent systematic review, published August 2023, which reviewed 12 RCTs and had 4,262 patients. This study revealed that targeted temperature of less than 37.5C, had better neurologic outcomes (RR 0.90 [0.83-0.98]) but no difference in overall mortality (RR 0.97 [0.90-1.06]).

A systematic review published in 2023 with 4058 patients showed that therapeutic hypothermia improved neurologic outcomes for patients who initially had a shockable rhythm and therapy was initiated early (<120 min) and was prolonged for at least 24 hours.
While strict glucose control has been recommended in patients after sudden cardiac arrest, the best study to date of this practice in ICU patients in general did not find a benefit (NICE-SUGARY).
There is no evidence for the use of corticosteroid supplementation for relative adrenal insufficiency in cardiac arrest victims.

There is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of prophylactic antiarrhythmic drugs in survivors of cardiac arrest; however, continuing an infusion associated with the return of spontaneous circulation is reasonable.
Witnessed seizures should be treated. There are insufficient data to make a recommendation regarding routine seizure prophylaxis.

In a recent randomized control trial published in American Journal of Emergency Medicine in 2023 studied 746 participants with hypercapnia after cardiac arrest and concluded that the rate of change in PaCO2 was not associated with improved functional outcome, however there was a trend that higher decreased rate of PaCO2 was associated with increased mortality. A few months later in the NEJM in 2023, they studied the effect of mild hypercapnia in adults who remained comatose after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The pathophysiology behind hypercapnia, it vasodilates cerebral blood vessels, improving cerebral blood flow and was thought to improve neurological outcomes. They studied 1700 participants to a PaCO2 target of 50-55 mmHg for 24 hours and found that there was no difference in better neurologic outcomes at 6 months when compared to normocapnia.

Prognostic signs that strongly predict death/poor neurologic outcome include the absence of each of the following: corneal reflex, pupillary response, and withdrawal to pain. Absence of motor response at 24 hours and then at 72 hours also portends a poor prognosis.

In a recent systematic review and meta-analysis published in Critical Care Medicine in 2021, analyzed 39 studies (n=17,179), and concluded that using early quantitative pupillary light reflex had similar specificity to late standard pupillary light reflex and can assist in neurologic prognostication earlier in patients who remained comatose post-resuscitation.
Family members who witness out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation of a patient were not more likely to suffer post-traumatic stress disorder than controls.

For patients with out of hospital cardiac arrest without ST elevation on ECG, immediate coronary angiography does not improve outcomes when compared to deferred angiography (i.e., once neurologic function has improved).
Empiric antibiotics with amoxicillin-clavulanate reduces the incidence of early ventilator-associated pnuemonia (NNT=7) for patient treated with targeted temperature management.

In a recent randomized control trial in NEJM published in 2022, 789 participants were analyzed to a target mean arterial pressure of either 63 mmHg or 77 mmHg who were in a comatose state after being resuscitated after an out of hospital cardiac arrest and found there was no difference in mortality, having severe disability or change in comatose status.
Survivors of a life-threatening arrhythmic event not due to a transient or reversible cause benefit from implantable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy.

Pooled data from three randomized secondary prevention trials indicate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy reduces annual all-cause mortality from 12.3% per year to 8.8% per year (NNT: 29 to save 1 life per year of follow-up).
Antiarrhythmic drug therapy did not reduce sudden cardiac death risk in these clinical trials.

Approximately 3% to 15% of sudden cardiac arrest victims treated by emergency personnel survive to hospital discharge. The highest survival is in those patients with ventricular fibrillation.
Among survivors, a minority demonstrate memory and learning impairment; most are highly functioning.
Survival following out-of-hospital arrest without the return of spontaneous circulation at the scene is exceedingly rare.

In hospital arrest is associated with a 18% survival to discharge, but among those elderly patients who are successfully resuscitated, 60% are alive at 1 year and 44% at 3 years. Predictors of failed resuscitation in the hospital setting include advanced age (<80 years), nursing home as usual residence, impaired renal function, and active diagnosis of malignancy. A clinical decision rule can identify patients at low and very low likelihood of a good outcome following attempted resuscitation (GO-FAR score).
Only 27% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest victims receive bystander CPR.

In a European study of out-of-hospital CPR performed by medical personnel, chest compressions, when indicated, were not performed 48% of the time. In addition, compression depth was satisfactory in less than one third of cases.
Mortality from in-hospital arrest is highest during nights and weekends.
A recent systematic review found that approximately 1 in 5 elderly victims of in hospital cardiac arrest survive to hospital dischage.
The MIRACLE2 risk score used 7 predictors to identify patients at low (5.6%), moderate (55%), and high (92%) risk of a poor outcome following out of hospital cardiac arrest.

A systematic review with meta-analysis in 2022 revealed a 24% survival-to-discharge rate, 18% of patients had a favorable neurologic outcome with the use of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR). This study suggested that ECPR is a promising resource for increasing survival rates.

A randomized control trial published in January 2023 revealed that patients with refractory out of hospital cardiac arrest, ECPR versus conventional CPR had similar survival rates but with better neurological outcomes.

feature.caption: Noncoronary Heart Disease Substrates for Sudden Cardiac Arrest.
feature.feature_body:
Substrate Distinguishing Features
Valvular heart disease Risk of sudden cardiac arrest in patients with asymptomatic aortic stenosis is low. Sudden cardiac death is the second leading mode of death after valve replacement surgery.
Congenital heart disease1
Ventricular tachycardia is common in Tetralogy of Fallot and as a late complication after surgical repair of complex lesions.
Congenital coronary anomalies Anomalous origin of a left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery or from the right/noncoronary cusp, passing between the aortic and pulmonary artery roots.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Asymmetric left ventricular hypertrophy involving the interventricular septum, may be associated with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Autosomal dominant; most common mutations in the β-myosin heavy chain and a-tropomyosin.
Brugada syndrome The most diagnostic electrocardiographic abnormality is >2 mm of ST-segment elevation in a right precordial lead. The following drugs may aggravate the ST-segment elevation and are contraindicated: class IA and IC agents, calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers, nitrates, tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia Cardiomyopathy associated with sudden death in young people and adults; often precipitated by exercise. Characterized by 2 pathological patterns: fatty and fibrofatty infiltration of myocardium. ECG abnormalities: epsilon waves, localized prolongation of the QRS in the right precordial leads; inverted Ts in right precordial leads; incomplete right bundle branch block.
Long QT syndrome May be congenital or acquired. There are at least 7 genes implicated in long QT syndrome (LQTS) and each may have a different influence on clinical course. The 3 most common LQTS genotypes, accounting for about 45% of LQTS, are LQT1, LQT2 (both potassium channel gene mutations), and LQT3 (a sodium channel gene mutation).
Short QT syndrome Characterized by a shortened QT interval and by episodes of syncope, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation or life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Typically affects young and healthy people with no structural heart disease. May be present in sporadic cases as well as in families.
Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia VT/VF as a result of emotional or physical stress without underlying structural HD. Often brought out during exercise testing.
Commotio cordis Precipitated by a sudden blow to the precordium, typically occurring during a 20 msec window on the upslope of the T-wave.
Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation No apparent structural heart disease. Thought to occur in ~5% of victims of sudden cardiac death (sudden cardiac death).
Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome ECG: short PR interval, delta waves. Mechanism of sudden cardiac death likely secondary to development of AF rapidly conducting through accessory pathway and degenerating to ventricular fibrillation.

feature.feature_body:
Hypothermia Protocol Post Arrest Use for 24 hours Starting at Time Cooling Begins
Date Time
Inclusion Criteria (MUST Have ALL):
18 years or older. Initial rhythm ventricular fibrillation/pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Mechanically ventilated. Systolic B/P greater than 90 spontaneously or with IV fluids. Women—negative pregnancy test unless postmenopausal. Comatose. Temperature greater than 35.6ºC after arrest.
Exclusion Criteria (If Patient Meets Any of the Below: NOT a Candidate)
Traumatic cardiac arrest. DNR status/terminal illness. Admission wt less than 50 kg. SpO2 less than 90% on 100% O2. Pregnant (+test). Sepsis/ongoing infection. Acute pulmonary edema. Unstable rhythm. Surgery prior 14 day. paO2 less than 69 mmHg on 100% O2. Active GI bleed. Coagulopathy.
Cardiology consult. CBC admission, 12 hours and 24 hours. BMP (glucose, BUN, creatinine, Na, K, CO2, calcium) on admission, 12 hours and 24 hours. Magnesium on admission, 12 hours and 24 hours. Pregnancy test for women less than 50 years old. Insert temperature sensing foley catheter. If pulmonary artery catheter is place utilize Core temperature readings. Record Core Body Temperature. If temperature less than 35ºC, do not proceed with protocol. Record temperature and vital signs every hour for 24 hours. Establish IV access. Titrate intervention to maintain GOAL TEMPERATURE of 33ºC as follows:
If temperature greater than 34ºC:
Turn off ventilator heater. Decrease room thermostat. Place cooling blanket under patient. Set blanket temperature to 0ºC. Place 6 ice packs on patient: under neck, 1 on top of neck, in each axilla, 1 in each groin. Place cooling blanket over patient. Medications:
Initiate Adult Ventilator Protocol orders. Initiate Adult Ventilator Sedation orders. Bolus Vecuronium 0.1 mg/kg IV x1, begin infusion at 1 mcg/kg/min and titrate to Goal of 2/4 Train of Four (TOF) Guidelines for Vecuronium Titration:
0/4–1/4 TOF, rate of infusion should be decreased by 1 ml/hr. 2/4 TOF, rate of infusion remains the same. 3/4–4/4 TOF, rate of infusion should be increase by 1 ml/hr. Maintain paralytic and sedation until temperature of 36ºC is reached: Discontinue paralysis and discontinue Midazolam once TOF of 4/4 is achieved. Observe for hypotension and hyperkalemia during rewarming. CBC once normothermic (36ºC). BMP once normothermic (36ºC).
